title: What is the difference between Flink SQL and Spark SQL for streaming use cases — Flink SQL is true continuous/incremental processing with native changelog semantics; Spark SQL (Structured Streaming) is micro-batch by default (or experimental continuous mode) — and what are the trade-offs (latency, exactly-once, state management, ecosystem)?
shortTitle: What is the difference between Flink SQL and Spark SQL for streaming use cases

s1_definition.profdef: Flink SQL and Spark Structured Streaming are both SQL-style engines for processing streaming data, but their core execution models differ. Flink is a true streaming engine: it processes each event as it arrives through a continuously running dataflow, with native event-time windowing, watermarks, and changelog semantics that model inserts, updates, and deletes as first-class retract and upsert streams. Spark Structured Streaming is micro-batch by default: it collects incoming data into small batches on a trigger interval and runs each batch as an incremental query over Spark's engine, which gives very high throughput and a unified batch-and-stream API but adds the batch interval as a floor on latency. Spark also has an experimental continuous-processing mode for lower latency, but the mainstream production model is micro-batch.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India processing transactions. Flink is like a teller who handles every customer the instant they walk up to the counter, one by one, continuously, so a transaction is reflected within milliseconds. Spark micro-batch is like a teller who lets a short queue form for, say, one second, then processes the whole queue together, then the next queue. The batched teller is extremely efficient at pushing through huge volumes, but any single customer waits at least until the next batch. For a live fraud alert that must fire in milliseconds, the continuous teller wins; for a massive end-of-second analytics roll-up, the batched teller is often simpler and just as good.
s1_definition.oneliner: Flink SQL is true event-at-a-time streaming with native changelog semantics and millisecond latency; Spark Structured Streaming is micro-batch by default, trading a batch-interval latency floor for a unified batch-stream engine and huge throughput.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Flink SQL and Spark Structured Streaming are both SQL-style engines for processing streaming data, but their core execution models differ. Flink is a true streaming engine: it processes each event as it arrives through a continuously running dataflow, with native event-time windowing, watermarks, and changelog semantics that model inserts, updates, and deletes as first-class retract and upsert streams. Spark Structured Streaming is micro-batch by default: it collects incoming data into small batches on a trigger interval and runs each batch as an incremental query over Spark's engine, which gives very high throughput and a unified batch-and-stream API but adds the batch interval as a floor on latency. Spark also has an experimental continuous-processing mode for lower latency, but the mainstream production model is micro-batch.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India processing transactions. Flink is like a teller who handles every customer the instant they walk up to the counter, one by one, continuously, so a transaction is reflected within milliseconds. Spark micro-batch is like a teller who lets a short queue form for, say, one second, then processes the whole queue together, then the next queue. The batched teller is extremely efficient at pushing through huge volumes, but any single customer waits at least until the next batch. For a live fraud alert that must fire in milliseconds, the continuous teller wins; for a massive end-of-second analytics roll-up, the batched teller is often simpler and just as good.

**One line to remember:** Flink SQL is true event-at-a-time streaming with native changelog semantics and millisecond latency; Spark Structured Streaming is micro-batch by default, trading a batch-interval latency floor for a unified batch-stream engine and huge throughput.

sections.s2_technical:
The fundamental difference is the execution model. Flink runs a long-lived dataflow graph where operators are always on and each record flows through as it arrives. Windowing, joins, and aggregations are driven by event time and watermarks, and Flink's Table API and SQL compile to this continuous runtime. Spark Structured Streaming, by contrast, models a stream as an unbounded table and repeatedly runs an incremental batch query triggered every interval, for example every one second, so each trigger processes the data that arrived since the last trigger. This means Spark's minimum latency is roughly the trigger interval plus processing time, typically hundreds of milliseconds to seconds, whereas Flink can achieve single-digit to tens of milliseconds because there is no batch boundary to wait for.

Changelog semantics are a major distinction. Flink natively represents updates as retract streams, with update-before and update-after rows, and upsert streams keyed by a primary key, so aggregations over changing data, CDC ingestion, and temporal joins are all first-class. Spark's streaming model is more oriented toward append and complete or update output modes, and while it supports stateful aggregations and stream-stream joins, it does not have the same native changelog-and-retract machinery, so some update-heavy patterns are more natural in Flink. On state management, Flink has rich keyed state with pluggable backends including RocksDB for very large state spilled to disk, fine-grained state time-to-live, and incremental checkpoints, which suits large, long-lived streaming state. Spark keeps state in a state store checkpointed to the file system and is very capable, but its state model is tied to the micro-batch structure.

On exactly-once, both deliver it but differently. Flink uses asynchronous distributed checkpoints based on the Chandy-Lamport algorithm, aligning barriers across the dataflow, and combines them with transactional or idempotent sinks to give end-to-end exactly-once. Spark achieves exactly-once through checkpointing offsets plus a write-ahead log and idempotent or transactional sinks per batch. The ecosystem trade-off matters too: Spark has an enormous unified ecosystem spanning batch ETL, SQL, machine learning with MLlib, and a single API for batch and streaming, which is attractive when a team already runs Spark for everything and wants one tool. Flink is more specialised for streaming and shines where low latency, complex event-time handling, CDC, and large evolving state dominate. The senior nuances are these. First, choose Flink when latency must be in the low tens of milliseconds, when you need native CDC and retract semantics, or when state is huge and long-lived. Second, choose Spark when you want one engine for both batch and streaming, when your latency budget is seconds, or when you lean on the Spark and MLlib ecosystem. Third, Spark's continuous mode narrows the latency gap but has historically been experimental with feature limits. Fourth, both scale horizontally, so the decision is rarely about raw throughput and almost always about latency, semantics, and ecosystem fit. Knowing that the choice is a trade-off driven by requirements, not a claim that one is universally better, is what marks a mature engineer.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India must raise a fraud alert within tens of milliseconds of a suspicious transaction, because a delayed alert lets a fraudulent withdrawal complete. A micro-batch engine that waits for a one-second batch boundary adds a full second of latency before the alert can even be computed. This is exactly the latency difference between true streaming and micro-batch.

Problem 2 — The same bank also produces an end-of-second analytics roll-up of total transaction value per branch for a management dashboard, where a one-second cadence is perfectly acceptable and extremely high throughput matters more than millisecond latency. This is exactly where a micro-batch engine is a natural and simple fit.

In the mini-project we build a runnable demo that contrasts the two execution models on the same transaction stream. We define a `Txn` with an amount and an arrival time, a `ContinuousProcessor` that handles each transaction the instant it arrives and records its processing latency, and a `MicroBatchProcessor` that buffers transactions and only processes them when the batch interval elapses, recording the added batching latency. A `EngineComparisonDemo` main class feeds the same transactions to both, prints per-transaction latencies, and summarises the average latency difference, making the trade-off concrete.

The equivalent SQL on each engine:

```sql
-- flink_query.sql : Flink SQL, continuous, per-event fraud filter
SELECT txn_id, account_id, amount
FROM transactions
WHERE amount > 500000;   -- emitted the instant such a txn arrives
```

```sql
-- spark_query.sql : Spark Structured Streaming, micro-batch roll-up
-- spark.readStream ... .trigger(Trigger.ProcessingTime("1 second"))
SELECT window(event_time, '1 second') AS w, branch, SUM(amount) AS total
FROM transactions
GROUP BY window(event_time, '1 second'), branch;
```

sections.s5_journey:
The input is five transactions arriving at zero, two hundred, four hundred, six hundred, and eight hundred milliseconds. T1 and T4 exceed the fraud threshold of five hundred thousand.

Step 1. In the continuous engine, T1 at six hundred thousand is processed the instant it arrives at time zero. Its latency is essentially zero, and because it exceeds the threshold a fraud alert fires immediately. This is the behaviour a real fraud system needs.

Step 2. T2, T3, T4, and T5 are each processed at their own arrival times, with near-zero latency. T4 at six hundred thousand fires a second fraud alert at six hundred milliseconds. The continuous engine's average latency is about zero, because no event waits for anything.

Step 3. In the micro-batch engine, the five transactions are buffered as they arrive. None is processed yet, because the batch has not triggered. The data sits in the buffer.

Step 4. At one thousand milliseconds the batch interval elapses and the whole batch fires together. Every transaction is processed in one pass, which is efficient, but each one's latency is measured from its arrival to the one-second trigger. T1, which arrived at time zero, has a latency of one thousand milliseconds; T5, which arrived at eight hundred, has two hundred. The average latency is several hundred milliseconds, dominated by the wait for the batch boundary.

Step 5. The demo prints both averages. The continuous engine's average is near zero while the micro-batch engine's average is in the hundreds of milliseconds. This makes the core trade-off concrete: for a millisecond-sensitive fraud alert the continuous model wins, while for a one-second roll-up the batch model's latency is irrelevant and its throughput efficiency is attractive.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Flink SQL and Spark Structured Streaming are both SQL-style streaming engines, but they differ at the core in how they execute. Flink is a true streaming engine: operators run continuously and each event flows through the dataflow the instant it arrives, with native event-time windowing, watermarks, and changelog semantics where inserts, updates, and deletes are first-class retract and upsert streams. Spark Structured Streaming is micro-batch by default: it treats the stream as an unbounded table and re-runs an incremental batch query every trigger interval, so it is extremely efficient and gives a unified batch-and-stream API, but the trigger interval becomes a floor on latency. Spark has an experimental continuous mode that narrows the gap, but the mainstream production model is micro-batch.

The trade-offs fall into four areas. On latency, Flink reaches single-digit to tens of milliseconds because nothing waits for a batch boundary, while Spark micro-batch is typically hundreds of milliseconds to seconds. On semantics, Flink's native retract and upsert streams make CDC ingestion, update-heavy aggregations, and temporal joins first-class, whereas Spark leans on append, complete, and update output modes and does not have the same native changelog machinery. On state, Flink offers rich keyed state with pluggable backends like RocksDB for very large state, fine-grained time-to-live, and incremental checkpoints, which suits huge long-lived state, while Spark's capable state store is tied to the micro-batch structure. Both provide exactly-once, Flink through asynchronous distributed checkpoints plus transactional sinks and Spark through offset checkpointing plus a write-ahead log and idempotent sinks. The ecosystem is Spark's great strength: one engine for batch, SQL, and machine learning, which is compelling if a team already runs Spark for everything.

At the National Bank of India I used both deliberately, because the choice is about requirements, not one being universally better. For fraud detection, where an alert must fire within tens of milliseconds or a fraudulent withdrawal completes, I used Flink SQL, because its true per-event processing meant a suspicious transaction triggered an alert the instant it arrived, with no batch delay, and its native changelog semantics let me ingest CDC from the accounts database cleanly. For the end-of-second management dashboard that rolled up total transaction value per branch, I used Spark Structured Streaming, because a one-second cadence was perfectly acceptable, the micro-batch model gave excellent throughput, and the team already used Spark and MLlib for the risk-scoring models feeding that dashboard, so one engine covered batch, streaming, and machine learning. Being able to explain that Flink is true streaming with native changelog and millisecond latency, that Spark is micro-batch with a unified ecosystem, and to justify choosing each by latency, semantics, state, and ecosystem fit, is exactly what shows I select streaming technology by engineering requirements rather than fashion.
